claims.text: A controlled dual-phase microstructure containing a low-density matrix and dispersed nanoscale oxide-forming precipitates will synergistically improve strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to a homogeneous alloy.
The initial alloy is a homogeneous single-phase lightweight high-entropy alloy optimized for low density.
Thermomechanical processing can induce controlled phase partitioning in the proposed alloy.
The processing will produce a continuous lightweight matrix containing uniformly dispersed nanoscale oxide-forming precipitates.
The matrix–precipitate interfaces act as a protective network.
Dispersed precipitates nucleate stable protective oxide phases at elevated temperatures.
The dispersed precipitates reinforce the matrix and contribute to mechanical strengthening.
The precipitate-containing microstructure impedes corrosive attack.
Engineered phase partitioning preserves the alloy's low density.
Engineered phase partitioning overcomes trade-offs between low weight and multi-property performance.
The processed dual-phase alloy will have higher yield strength than the homogeneous baseline.
The processed dual-phase alloy will have better corrosion resistance than the homogeneous baseline.
The processed dual-phase alloy will have better high-temperature oxidation performance than the homogeneous baseline.
At sufficiently high temperatures, precipitate coarsening will diminish the proposed benefits.
Degradation of the nanoscale oxide network will cause the hypothesis to cease to hold.
Prior observations support effects of microstructure and elemental segregation on oxidation and corrosion behavior.
The proposed comparison holds alloy composition constant and varies the thermomechanically induced microstructure.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in all three target properties would falsify the hypothesis.
An improvement in one target property offset by degradation in another would falsify the proposed synergy.
